opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me first was how interdisciplinary it felt. I came from a pure math background, so I was used to a culture where you sit alone with a problem for weeks. At Oxford, the computational neuroscience people were constantly mixing. You'd have a physicist, a clinician, a machine learning person, and someone running wet-lab experiments all in the same reading group, arguing about the same question from completely different angles.

The other thing that excited me was the questions themselves. They were very fundamental. How does the brain represent abstract structure? How do we generalize from so little data? How does something like a "cognitive map" get built? To me, those felt deeply connected to mathematics. Even though there's messy biology underneath, people were looking for principles, for structure, and that's the part I've always loved.

There was also a real openness to theory. In some places theory is treated as secondary to experiments. In the UK community I met, a clean model that made a surprising prediction was celebrated. That gave someone like me, a math person who wasn't trained as a biologist, room to contribute.

And looking back, it was formative for how I think about AI now. Seeing how people tried to reverse-engineer reasoning in the brain made me ask: if we want machines that truly reason, especially in something as rigorous as mathematics, what kind of structure do they need? That question has stayed with me ever since.

fable-5.1.text:
I think what struck me most was how genuinely interdisciplinary it was, and not in the way people usually use that word, where it's really just one field borrowing a tool from another. At Cambridge and Oxford, the people doing computational neuroscience were sitting in the same rooms as mathematicians, physicists, and experimental biologists, and they were all asking the same question from different directions: how does a physical system made of neurons give rise to something like learning or memory or reasoning?

Coming from a mathematics background, I was used to a culture where you prove things and the problem is closed. In neuroscience the problem is almost never closed. The brain doesn't hand you clean axioms. So you have this community that is extremely rigorous mathematically, people who care deeply about dynamical systems, information theory, Bayesian inference, and at the same time they are humble in front of the data. They'll build a beautiful model and then say, well, the mouse disagrees, so let's go back. I found that combination really exciting. It's rigor without arrogance.

The other thing was the tradition. The UK has this long lineage going back to people like Horace Barlow and David Marr, this idea that you should think about what computation the brain is actually trying to perform, at the level of the problem, before you dive into mechanism. That framing shaped how I think about intelligence in general, including artificial intelligence. It made me ask not just "can we make a system that works" but "what is the structure of the problem this system is solving, and why would any solution look the way it does." That question has stayed with me, and honestly it's part of why I ended up working on mathematical reasoning and AI. The brain is the one existence proof we have that a physical system can do mathematics, so studying how it might do that felt like the most natural bridge between the two things I cared about.

astra-6.text: What excited me was how interdisciplinary it felt. You had people coming at the same questions from mathematics, computer science, and neuroscience, and those different perspectives could really inform one another. I was especially drawn to the possibility of turning a question about the brain into a mathematical model—and then asking whether that model actually explains what we observe. That interplay between abstract ideas and empirical evidence was really exciting to me.
